(Guangzhou, China). BODIPY-cholesterol (HY-125746), Probucol (HY-B0388), ApoA-I (HY-P72833), and BLT-1 (HY-116767) were obtained from MedChemExpress (MCE).

Cell lines and animals
The RAW264.7 murine macrophage cell line and the mouse embryonic fibroblasts line (NIH 3T3) were purchased from the Chinese Academy of Sciences Cells Bank (Shanghai, China). The human umbilical vein endothelial cell line (HUVEC) was purchased from Cyagen Biosciences (Guangzhou, China) Inc. All cells were cultivated in a humidified atmosphere at 37 °C with 5% of CO .

C57BL/6 mice (6 weeks, female) were purchased from Beijing Vital River Laboratory Animal Technology. ApoE−/− mice (6 weeks, female) were purchased from SPF (Beijing) Biotechnology Co., Ltd. High-fat diet (HFD) feeding of AopE−/− mice began at six weeks of age. All mice were housed in the same specific pathogen-free (SPF) facility and maintained under identical environmental parameters, including cage type, temperature (25 °C), humidity, handling procedures, and a 12-hour light/dark cycle. All model groups received the same HFD throughout the study, and food and water were provided ad libitum, with diet replaced twice weekly. The high-fat diet used in this study was sourced from SPF (Beijing) Biotechnology Co., Ltd., catalog number SFD004. The diet has an energy density of 4.7 kcal/g, with 41% of total kcal from fat, 42% from carbohydrate, and 17% from protein. By weight, the diet contained 21.2% lard, 49.1% carbohydrates, 19.8% protein, and 0.2% cholesterol. Carbohydrates in the formulation are primarily composed of corn starch, sucrose, and maltodextrin, and the fiber component contains 31 g/kg crude fiber based on 90% dry matter. The primary sources of fat are lard (42% saturated fatty acids, 48% monounsaturated fatty acids, 10% polyunsaturated fatty acids) and soybean oil (15% saturated fatty acids, 24% monounsaturated fatty acids, 61% polyunsaturated fatty acids). The diet contains 0.2% cholesterol by weight (equivalent to 2 g/kg), and sodium cholate is not included in the formulation. All procedures involving animals were conducted by the guidelines set by the Tianjin Committee of Use and Care of Laboratory Animals, and approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of Nankai University (2024-SYDWLL-000693).

Characterizations
1H and 13C nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra were acquired using a Bruker-DPX 400 spectrometer. High-resolution mass spectra (HRMS) were performed on a Bruker AutoflexIII LRF200-CID mass spectrometer in matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight (MALDI-TOF) mode. The absorption spectra were detected using a Shimadzu UV-1800 spectrometer. Edinburgh FS5 was used to measure the photoluminescence (PL) spectra. Transmission electron microscope (TEM) images were captured using a Talos L120C G2 instrument by FEI, Czech. Dynamic light scattering (DLS) measurements were performed on a Malvern Zeta sizer Nano ZS-90. PA imaging was conducted on a commercial small-animal optoacoustic tomography system (Vevo LAZR, FujiFilm VisualSonics, America). A short-wavelength infrared (SWIR) imaging system (Wuhan Grand-imaging Technology Co., LTD) was utilized for NIR-II fluorescence imaging of animals and organs. A bruker 9.4 T BioSpec 94/30 MRI installations for small animal magnetic resonance imaging test.

Fabrication of nanoformulations
First, RAW264.7 cells were dispersed in the membrane protein extraction reagent (Beyotime, China) containing 1 mM PMSF and cooled down at 4 °C for 30 min, and subsequently broken by ultrasound (80 W) for 10 min. The mixture was repeatedly frozen and thawed at −80 °C and 37 °C for 3 times, and then centrifuged at 3,000 g for 10 min. The resulting supernatant was centrifugated at 12,000 g × 10 min, followed by a final centrifugation at 100,000 g for 1 h to obtain membrane in precipitates. The membrane was stored at −80 °C for further use.

The targeting molecule (DSPE-PEG-CLIKKPF) was synthesized according to previous reports.[28,67] Briefly, CLIKKPF was reacted with DSPE-PEG-maleimide via thiol-Michael addition reaction in water/methanol solution (90:10, v/v) for 8 h at room temperature. Then the residual CLIKKPF peptide was removed by centrifugal filters (Merck Millipore Co., Ltd, Shanghai China) and the final product DSPE-PEG-CLIKKPF was obtained by lyophilizing.

The molecular probe and AT-loaded nanoformulations were fabricated using a modified nanoprecipitation technique. The synthesis was carried out at 20 °C, where FTBGd (1 mg), AT (1 mg), DSPE-PEG (2 mg), and PPADT (4 mg) were dissolved in 1 mL of DMSO under constant stirring. After achieving complete dissolution, the resulting stock solution was gradually introduced into 15 mL of deionized water under vigorous stirring. During nanoprecipitation, DSPE-PEG was incorporated as a stabilizing surfactant. Owing to its amphiphilic structure, DSPE-PEG anchors its hydrophobic lipid tail within the nanoparticle core while presenting a hydrophilic PEG corona on the surface, thereby enhancing colloidal stability. To eliminate the organic solvent, the mixture underwent dialysis against water for 12 h using a dialysis membrane with an MWCO of 3,500 Da, ultimately producing the final solution, termed FA-P. The encapsulation efficiencies of FTBGd and AT were found to be 63.7% and 59.5%, respectively. To synthesize FA-P@M, a solution of FA-P (100 \muL, 1 mg mL‒1 based on FTBGd) was combined with 0.5 mg of membrane and subjected to ultrasound treatment (100 W, 50 Hz) for 5 min. The mixture was then repeatedly extruded through a micro-extruder with a 200 nm pore size to form FA-P@M. Uncoated membranes were eliminated by centrifugation at 3,000 g, followed by washing until no residual protein was detected in the supernatant. The obtained FA-P@M was stored at 4 °C for future use. After obtaining FA-P@M, FA-P@MC was prepared by incorporating DSPE-PEG-CLIKKPF into its lipid membrane.

Drug release from FA-P@MC
The AT release profile from FA-P@MC or FA-P was investigated under varying H O levels (0, 2.5 \muM, 0.1 mM, 1.0 mM, or 1.0 mM + catalase). Prior to the release studies, both nanoformulations were confirmed to exhibit similar particle sizes and identical drug loading, ensuring a valid comparison. 2 mg of FA-P@MC or FA-P was suspended in 5 mL of deionized water and sealed inside a dialysis bag (MWCO = 10,000). This bag was subsequently submerged in 15 mL of buffer solution and placed in a shaker set to 37 °C with a rotation speed of 30 × g. At predetermined time points, 2 mL of the incubation medium was withdrawn for HPLC analysis, and an equivalent volume of fresh medium was added back to the buffer solution. The percentage of cumulative AT release was determined using the equation: Cumulative drug release (%) = (M/M ) × 100%, where M represents the drug quantity released at time t, and M corresponds to the initial drug content in FA-P@MC. All release experiments were performed in triplicate.

The H O levels in plaque tissues were measured using a commercially available Hydrogen Peroxide Content Assay Kit (Solarbio, BC3595), following the manufacturer's protocol. Briefly, freshly isolated plaque tissues were homogenized in the supplied buffer on ice and centrifuged, and the resulting supernatants were used for analysis. Absorbance was measured at 415 nm using a UV–Vis spectrophotometer (SHIMADZU), and H O concentrations were calculated based on a standard curve generated with known H O standards. The results are reported as mean ± SD (n = 6 individual plaque samples), yielding an H O level of 0.34 ± 0.05 mM, corresponding to approximately 0.34 \mu mol per gram of wet tissue.

Cellular uptake behavior
Cellular uptake of different formulations by foam cells was evaluated. To generate foam cells, RAW264.7 cells were exposed to a medium supplemented with 50 \mug/mL oxLDL. Following this, the medium was substituted with fresh medium containing DiI-labeled nanoparticles—FA-P, FA-P@M, or FA-P@MC—at an FTGd concentration of 50 \muM. After incubation, the cells underwent three PBS washes, were fixed using 4% tissue fixative for 15 min, and then washed three additional times with PBS. The nuclei were stained with DAPI for 10 min, followed by another PBS wash to eliminate residual dye. Finally, confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) (LSM 800 with Airyscan, ZEISS, Germany) was utilized for imaging, and analysis was conducted using ZEN 2012 software.

The transmigration of the NPs across inflamed HUVECs and their subsequent uptake by foam cells were evaluated using in vitro transwell migration assays. HUVECs were cultured in the upper chamber of a Transwell insert (0.3 \mu m) and exposed to 1 \mug/mL LPS for 24 h to induce an inflammatory response. At the same time, RAW264.7 cells (1 × 105 per well) were seeded in the lower chamber of a 24-well plate and treated with 50 \mug/mL oxLDL for 24 h to form foam cells. Subsequently, FA-P, FA-P@M, or FA-P@MC (50 \muM based on FTGd) were added to the upper chamber and incubated for 4 h. After incubation, the foam cells were rinsed three times with PBS and stained with DAPI for 15 min. Imaging was carried out using CLSM, and flow cytometry (BD LSR Fortessa, USA) was used for quantitative analysis.

In vitro safety evaluation
The cytotoxicity of FA-P@MC was evaluated in vitro using MTT assays with NIH 3T3 and HUVEC cell lines. In brief, the cells were plated in a 96-well plate at a concentration of 1 × 105 cells/mL. After 24 h of incubation, the medium was replaced with fresh medium containing nanoparticles at varying concentrations (0, 20, 40, 60, 80, and 100 \muM). Following another 24-hour incubation period, 100 \muL of MTT solution was added to each well. After 4 h, the MTT solution was removed, and 150 \muL of DMSO was added to each well, followed by shaking at room temperature. The optical density at 570 nm was then recorded using a microplate reader. For the LDH cytotoxicity assay, cells were exposed to various concentrations of the nanoparticle formulation. LDH release was then quantified using an LDH Cytotoxicity Assay Kit (Leagene Biotechnology Co., Ltd.) following the manufacturer’s instructions.

In vitro anti-inflammatory effect
Macrophages were simultaneously treated with 50 \mug/mL ox-LDL and different drug formulations (free AT, A-P, FA-P, FA-P@M, and FA-P@MC) at a concentration of 50 \muM for 24 h. After the treatment, the cells were washed three times with PBS. To assess intracellular ROS, the cells were incubated with 10 \muM of DCFH-DA in the dark. After removing the excess probe, the cells were further incubated at 37 °C for 30 min. Confocal microscopy was employed with 488 nm excitation and 530 ± 20 nm emission to observe the dichlorofluorescein (DCF) fluorescence resulting from the reaction of DCFH-DA with ROS. The release of nitric oxide (NO) from cells was assessed using the fluorescent NO probe, DAF-FM DA. The cells were treated with 50 \mug/mL ox-LDL and various drug formulations (free AT, A-P, FA-P, FA-P@M, and FA-P@MC) at a concentration of 50 \muM for 24 h, followed by three PBS washes. The NO probe, DAF-FM DA (final concentration: 5 \muM), was added, and the cells were incubated at 37 °C for 30 min, after which they were washed three times with PBS. Confocal microscopy was employed to visualize the cells. Statistical analysis and graphing were conducted using ZEN 2012 (Version 1.1.2.0).

Inhibition of lipid uptake and foam cell formation
RAW264.7 cells were seeded in confocal dishes at 1 × 105 cells per dish and allowed to adhere overnight. Cells were stimulated with 1 \mu g mL−1 of LPS for 6 h, followed by treatment with different formulations for an additional 12 h. Subsequently, cells were incubated with 50 \mu g mL−1 of DiI-oxLDL for 4 h. The cells were then washed with PBS, and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde. Fluorescence imaging was performed using CLSM to evaluate the cellular uptake of oxLDL. The expressions of CD36 and LOX-1 were evaluated by immunofluorescence using primary antibodies against CD36 and LOX-1, followed by incubation with fluorescently labeled secondary antibodies.

For foam cell formation and lipid accumulation assays, RAW264.7 cells were seeded in 12-well plates at 1 × 105 cells per well. Cells were then treated with 50 \mu g mL−1 of oxLDL in combination with various formulations for 12 h. For Oil Red O (ORO) staining, the foam cells were treated with the freshly prepared ORO working solution for 15 min and then rinsed with 60% isopropanol. Images of the cells were captured using confocal microscopy. After imaging, ORO was extracted using isopropanol, and its absorbance was measured at 492 nm using a microplate reader. Cholesterol efflux was quantified by collecting culture supernatants post-treatment. The expressions of SR-BI and ABCA1 were evaluated by immunofluorescence using primary antibodies against SR-BI and ABCA1, followed by incubation with fluorescently labeled secondary antibodies.

For functional cholesterol efflux assay, foam cells were loaded with 1 \mu g/mL BODIPY-labeled cholesterol (HY-125746, MedChemExpress) for 6 h to allow intracellular labeling. After washing, cells were treated with FA-P@MC or relevant control formulations in the presence of ApoA-I (10 \mu g mL−1, ABCA1-dependent) or HDL (40 \mu g mL−1, SR-BI/ABCG1-associated, YB-003, Yiyuan biotechnology) as cholesterol acceptors in serum-free medium for 24 h. As a control, cells were pre-incubated with pharmacological inhibitors of ABCA1 (probucol, 20 \mu M) or SR-BI (BLT-1, 1 \mu M) for 2 hours prior to efflux to assess the contribution of these transporters. Fluorescence intensity was determined in both supernatant and cell lysate using a microplate reader (excitation/emission 485/510 nm). The percent of cholesterol efflux was calculated as (fluorescence in the supernatant/the sum of the fluorescence in the medium and the fluorescence remaining in the cells) × 100%. Parallel cholesterol efflux studies were also conducted in foam cells induced from bone marrow–derived macrophages (BMDMs). Bone marrow cells were flushed from femurs and tibias of 8-week-old C57BL/6 mice, filtered through a 70 \mu m strainer, and plated in RPMI 1640 supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% penicillin-streptomycin, and 20 ng/mL M-CSF. Cells were differentiated for 7 days at 37 °C with 5% CO and used for cholesterol efflux assays. Macrophage differentiation was confirmed by F4/80 immunostaining.

CD47 expression analysis and in vitro efferocytosis evaluation
RAW264.7 cells were incubated with 50 \mu g/mL oxLDL for 24 h, followed by treatment with different NPs for an additional 24 h. Cells were first harvested and lysed in RIPA buffer supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors. Protein concentration was determined using a BCA assay, and equal amounts of protein were mixed with 4 × loading buffer and denatured by heating at 95 °C for 10 min in a metal bath. Samples were then separated by 10% SDS-PAGE and electrotransferred onto a 0.4 \mu m PVDF membrane. The membrane was blocked with BSA in TBST (Tris-buffered saline with 0.1% Tween-20) for 1 h at room temperature to minimize nonspecific binding. The membrane was then incubated overnight at 4 °C with a primary antibody against CD47, while GAPDH was used as a loading control. Following three washes with TBST, membranes were incubated with horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature. Protein bands were visualized using an enhanced chemiluminescence detection system, and band intensities were quantified using ImageJ software to determine relative CD47 expression levels.

For phagocytosis study, bone marrow–derived macrophages (BMDMs) were labeled with CFSE to serve as phagocytic cells, while oxLDL-treated RAW264.7 cells were used as foam cells. BMDMs and foam cells were co-cultured for 6 h. Following incubation, the medium was discarded, and the cells were washed with PBS, then fixed with 4% formaldehyde for 15 min. Fluorescence images were acquired using CLSM. For flow cytometry, treated cells were washed with PBS, detached, and subsequently analyzed on a BD LSR Fortessa (USA). Flow cytometric data were analyzed using FlowJo version 10.8.1.

In vivo biosafety and pharmacokinetics analysis
To assess the potential toxicity of FA-P@MC, 6-week-old healthy C57BL/6 mice were intravenously injected with PBS or FA-P@MC (10 mg kg-1) by intravenous injection twice weekly for 2 weeks (Day 0–14). One week after treatment (Day 22), the mice were euthanized, and blood samples were collected for analysis. For long-term biosafety evaluation, mice received weekly intravenous injections of either PBS or FA-P@MC (10 mg/kg based on FTBGd) for seven weeks (Day 0–49). On Day 50, hematological parameters, including white blood cell count, red blood cell count, hemoglobin concentration, hematocrit, mean red blood cell volume, platelet count, mean corpuscular hemoglobin content, and mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration, were measured using an automated hematology analyzer. Serum samples were obtained to evaluate various biochemical markers in the blood, such as alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and creatinine concentrations. Additionally, key organs, including the heart, liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys, were collected for histopathological examination. In brief, tissues were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA), embedded in paraffin, and sliced into 5 \mu m sections for H&E staining. The stained tissue sections were subsequently analyzed using a digital microscope (Leica QWin).

For pharmacokinetic evaluation, 6-week-old C57BL/6 mice were given FA-P@MC intravenously at a dose of 10 mg/kg. Blood samples were taken at different time intervals (0, 4, 8, 12, 24, 48, and 72 h) from the inner eye socket following intravenous injection of different nanoparticles. The fluorescence intensity of the blood samples was quantified using a SWIR imaging system (Wuhan Grand-imaging Technology Co., LTD) to assess the plasma signals of the nanoparticles. The clearance of free AT in the bloodstream was determined by HPLC analysis. To study the in vivo metabolic fate and clearance routes, FA-P@MC was labeled with the near-infrared dye DiR. Fecal and urinary samples were collected at days 1, 3, and 7 after intravenous administration, and their fluorescence signals were monitored using IVIS.

Multimodal imaging and analysis of the aorta ex vivo
To perform ex vivo fluorescence and PA imaging of the aorta, ApoE−/− mice were fed a high-fat diet (HFD; SPF Biotechnology Co., Ltd., Beijing) for 12 weeks (Day 0–84) to induce atherosclerosis. On Day 85, atherosclerotic mice were intravenously administered FA-P@MC. Twelve hours after injection, the mice were euthanized, and the aortas were excised for ex vivo fluorescence and PA imaging to evaluate the probe’s ability to detect plaques and differentiate plaque severity. NIR-II fluorescence imaging was performed using a short-wave infrared (SWIR) system with 808 nm excitation and emission collected through a 1000 nm long-pass filter. PA imaging was acquired at 790 nm excitation using a VisualSonics Vevo LAZR multimodal imaging system (FUJIFILM VisualSonics, Canada). For fluorescence imaging, the laser power was 50 mW cm-2; for PA measurements, pulse energy = 20 mJ cm-2, frequency = 30 MHz, PA gain = 35 dB, pulse repetition rate = 20 Hz, and duration of pulsed laser = 7 ns. 790 nm was selected for PA imaging as it coincides with the probe’s absorption peak and yields strong PA responses. Endogenous absorbers such as hemoglobin exhibit reduced absorption in this spectral region compared to their strong visible-band absorption, and water shows low absorption at this wavelength before its absorption increases at longer wavelengths. For fluorescence imaging, 808 nm light was employed as the excitation source because the probe has strong absorption at this wavelength and can be efficiently excited using the widely available commercial 808 nm laser. This wavelength selection ensures sufficient excitation efficiency while maintaining compatibility with commonly available NIR laser. MRI was carried out on a 9.4 T small-animal MRI scanner (BioSpec 94/30, Bruker).

To validate the correlation between imaging signal intensities with plaque severity, the aorta was subsequently embedded in optimal cutting temperature (OCT) compound, frozen at −80 °C for 30 min, and sliced into 10 \mu m sections. For ORO staining, a working solution was prepared by diluting 6 mL of the stock solution with 4 mL of deionized water. Cryosections of the aorta were incubated with 10 \mu L of this solution for 2 to 5 min, then washed with 60% isopropanol and deionized water. Hematoxylin was used as a counterstain for 5 min. For immunofluorescence, sections were rinsed, blocked, and incubated with anti-F4/80 primary antibody (1:500, Bio-Rad, MCA497GA), followed by washing and incubation with fluorescently labeled secondary antibody for 60 min at room temperature. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI for 10 min. Images were acquired using a Zeiss fluorescence microscope (FITC: excitation at 488 nm; DAPI: excitation at 405 nm). For ROS staining, aorta sections were treated with DCFH-DA (10 \mu M) for 60 min at 37 °C, followed by a 10-min DAPI incubation at 37 °C. Fluorescent images of DCFH-DA were captured using a laser confocal microscope (DCFH-DA: excitation at 488 nm; DAPI: excitation at 405 nm).

In vivo NIR-II fluorescence, PA, and MR imaging
AopE-/- mice were fed a HDF for eight weeks (Day 0–56), and then received intravenous injections of FA-P@C, FA-P@M, or FA-P@MC (150 \mu L, 4 mg/kg based on FTBGd) via the tail vein on day 57. For the competitive blocking control, mice were pretreated with free CLIKKPF peptide (2 mg/kg, i.v.) 4 hours prior to FA-P@MC administration on Day 57. At predefined time points post nanoformulation injection (0, 3, 6, 12, 24, and 36 hours post-injection), mice were anesthetized with 2% isoflurane and then imaged using a SWIR system equipped with an InGaAs scientific-grade camera and a 1000 nm long-pass filter. To validate plaque visualization, a surgical incision was made to expose the carotid arteries. To evaluate drug distribution and plaque-targeting efficiency, atherosclerotic mice were intravenously administered Cy5-labeled AT, Cy5-AT-loaded FA-P@M, or Cy5-AT-loaded FA-P@MC on Day 57. Twelve hours post-injection, major organs and the aorta were harvested for ex vivo fluorescence imaging using an IVIS system. For quantitative analysis, tissues were weighed, homogenized, and centrifuged to collect supernatants. Cy5 fluorescence intensity in the supernatants was measured using a spectrofluorometer, and background fluorescence from untreated control tissues was subtracted. The AT content in each tissue was calculated based on a standard curve generated from known concentrations of Cy5-AT under identical conditions. To study lesion distribution, plaque tissues were cryosectioned, fixed with 4% PFA, permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100, and blocked with 5% BSA. Foam cells were identified by immunostaining with anti-F4/80 and counterstaining with BODIPY to visualize intracellular lipids. Additional staining was performed for PS (Sigma-Aldrich, 05-719, 1:200), CD68 (Abcam, ab283654, 1:200), and PLIN2 (Huabio, ET1704-17, 1:200) to evaluate co-localization with FA-P@MC. Images were acquired using a confocal laser scanning microscope under identical settings for all groups, and co-localization was analyzed using ImageJ.

PA imaging was conducted on living mice on day 57 (12 hours post-injection of different nanoprobe) using the VisualSonics Vevo LAZR multimodal system (Canada) under the following parameters: pulse energy = 20 mJ cm-2, wavelength range = 790 nm, frequency = 30 MHz, PA gain = 35 dB, pulse repetition rate = 20 Hz, and duration of pulsed laser = 7 ns. Ultrasound and PA signals were acquired simultaneously, and merged PA/US images were generated by overlaying pseudo-colored PA signals onto grayscale ultrasound images. MRI was performed on a 9.4T Bruker BioSpec 94/30 system before and 12 h post-injection of Gd-DOTA, FA-P@M, or FA-P@MC (150 \mu L, 4 mg/kg based on FTBGd) (day 57). Mice were anesthetized with 2% isoflurane and positioned in the MRI coil for baseline and post-injection scans. T1-weighted axial images were acquired for analysis.

In vivo therapeutic efficacy study
ApoE−/− mice were initially fed a high-fat diet for 8 weeks to induce the development of atherosclerotic plaques at arterial bifurcations (experimental days 0–56). On day 57, the atherosclerotic mice were randomly assigned to six treatment groups (n = 6 mice per group), including PBS, free AT, A-P, FA-P, FA-P@M, and FA-P@MC (at a dose of 3 mg/kg AT). Each group received intravenous injections of the designated treatment twice a week (days 57, 61, 64, 68, 71, 75, 78, 82, 85, 89, 92, 96, 99, 103, 106, and 110) while maintaining the high-fat diet for an additional 8 weeks (Day 57–112). A standard chow-fed control group was included for comparison. For the evaluation of therapeutic effects via in situ imaging at the end of treatment, mice were intravenously administered the FA-P@MC nanoprobe on Day 113. NIR-II fluorescence and PA imaging were performed 12 hours post-injection following the procedure described above. After imaging, mice were euthanized, and the entire aortas were carefully excised for subsequent analyses (Day 113). Atherosclerotic plaque burden was evaluated by ORO staining of the aortic arch, following established protocols as described above, to quantify lipid-rich plaque areas. Histological assessment of aortic root sections was performed after paraffin embedding. Sections were stained with H&E to examine general tissue morphology, while dihydroethidium (DHE) staining was applied to assess ROS levels within plaques. Immunofluorescence staining was carried out to evaluate the expression of CD47 and CD68, markers of phagocytosis and macrophage content, respectively. Plaque stability was further assessed by immunohistochemical staining of aortic root sections with Masson’s trichrome for collagen content, MMP-9 for matrix degradation, CD31 for angiogenesis, and \alpha-SMA for smooth muscle cell content. Quantitative analysis of stained sections was performed using Image-Pro Plus 6.0. The inflammation was evaluated by collecting fresh blood post-treatment, centrifuging to obtain serum, and measuring TNF-α and IL-6 levels using ELISA kits according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Immune cell profiling within plaques was performed by isolating plaque tissue, enzymatically digesting to obtain single-cell suspensions, and analyzing CD4+ (CD3+CD4+), CD8+ (CD3+CD8+), and regulatory T (Treg) cell (CD25+Foxp3+) populations using flow cytometry.

Statistical analysis
All data were presented as mean value ± the standard deviation of independent experiments. One-way ANOVA and two-way was utilized for statistical analysis. Values of *P ≤ 0.05, **P ≤ 0.01, ***P ≤ 0.001, and ****P ≤ 0.0001 were applied to annotate statistical significance.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The authors report a hierarchical nanoplatform for multimodal imaging and targeted therapy of atherosclerosis (AS). They
first constructed a molecular probe integrating MRI, NIR-II fluorescence, and PA imaging capabilities, enabling
comprehensive evaluation of atherosclerotic lesions and facilitating real-time monitoring of therapeutic outcomes. This
imaging probe was further combined with a therapeutic agent capable of enhancing lipid efflux and downregulating CD47
expression, ultimately leading to inhibition of plaque progression, attenuation of inflammation, and improvement of plaque
stability in AS mouse models. This research is interesting and holds promise for clinical application. Therefore, I suggest its
publication after some revisions, as detailed below.
Major points:
1. Although the authors have provided short-term biocompatibility data, the prolonged treatment course of AS necessitates
evaluation of long-term in vivo biosafety. It is also crucial to investigate the metabolic fate and clearance pathways of the
nanoplatform in vivo to assess the potential for accumulation or chronic toxicity.
2. The H2O2-responsive drug release is conducted on macrophage membrane-camouflaged nanoparticles. However, it is
not clear to me how much the envelope affects its drug-releasing ability, so the effect of H2O2 on nanoparticles without
macrophage encapsulation should be investigated.
3. The nanoparticle response was tested under H2O2 concentrations ranging from 0.01 to 1 mM. However, the physiological
concentration of H2O2 in atherosclerotic lesions is not clearly established. The authors should cite relevant literatures or
include justification for the selected concentration range to confirm its pathophysiological relevance.
4. Please clarify whether all experimental mice were fed the same high-fat diet throughout the study. A detailed description
of the composition and source of the high-fat diet would help in reproducing the study and understanding the model’s
robustness.
5. There appears to be an inconsistency between the 790 nm excitation used for PA imaging and the 808 nm excitation for
fluorescence imaging. The rationale for selecting these two close but distinct wavelengths should be addressed.
Minor points:
1. After the biomimetic modification, data on the nanoprobe's colloidal stability under physiological conditions should be
presented.
2. In Fig. 1c, the fluorescence intensity of the compounds increases in THF/water mixtures with a water fraction up to 95%.
The authors should explain this phenomenon.
3. In Figure 1m, need to give a clear response time.
4. Please add color bar in Fig. 8i.
5. In addition to the responsive polymer, the authors added DSPE-PEG to the system. What is the role of this polymer?

### Reviewer 2

The investigators have performed an elegant biomedical engineering feat- with a single molecule can be used for molecular
imaging to detect early atherosclerosis with 3 separate advanced imaging modalities- MRI, NIR-II, and photoacoustic
imaging.
They also perform elegant experiments in mouse models to demonstrate efficacy. This manuscript presents a scientifically
rigorous and impactful study, with strong translational potential. Addressing the mechanistic and quantitative gaps would
significantly strengthen the manuscript’s clarity.
My major concern is that this tool and approach does not take into consideration the reality of screening for early
atherosclerosis. The biggest cause of cardiovascular mortality is coronary artery disease. If a patient is asymptomatic-
screening even with established techniques as CACS, CT coronary angiography (+/- with photon counting capabilities) has
yet to be accepted. The proposal that a major unmet need is optimizing the performance of a molecular imaging contrast
agent for use in all three modalities of MRI, NIR-II and photoacoustic imaging is a ”significant challenge” relevant to
screening and treating early CAD is not well founded or backed up by reference to the current clinical literature. Whilst
carotid or peripheral artery disease may have some chances in the near future with techniques such as these- this fails to
accurately predict CAD and CAD-related MI/death. Thus, my concern is that this theranostic tool may not be addressing a
question that we need addressed from a diagnostic perspective.
In regard to potential therapeutic value of the tool, the investigators state that: probe, coupled with atorvastatin, is
encapsulated in responsive carriers, further camouflaged with macrophage membranes, and functionalized with a foam cell-
targeting peptide. The hierarchical targeting strategy leverages the biomimetic affinity of macrophages for inflamed plaques
and the selective targeting of foam cells through a phosphatidylserine (PS)-binding peptide, ensuring precise foam cell
navigation. The on-demand release of atorvastatin within foam cells promotes lipid efflux and reduces CD47 expression,
thereby enhancing macrophage-mediated phagocytosis. This intervention effectively inhibits plaque progression, alleviates
inflammation burden, and stabilizes plaques in AS mouse models”. This sounds fantastic, however, most of the steps
outlined in this, and what is shown in the graphical abstract, is not backed with specific experimental data and appropriate
controls, and is theoretical, based on the engineering. Eg. “while the targeting peptide directs the system to foam cells within
plaques. Atorvastatin release within foam cells promotes lipid efflux and reduces CD47 expression, thereby enhancing
macrophage-mediated phagocytosis”. Causality is implied here regarding the specific targeting release of atorvastatin within
foam cells promotes the lipid efflux and reduces CD47, thereby enhancing macrophage- mediated
phagocytosis. There are many layers of this that need specific control to declare causality. These are not well described in the abstract, or the
graphical abstract.
When the reader dives in, there is some effort to address this- particularly in regard to the
nanoparticle itself in the in vitro model of OxLDL induced endothelial inflammation and
foam cell interaction. While Western blotting confirms the presence of
macrophage membrane proteins like F4/80, there's no quantification done on the peptide density or coating efficiency on the
cells. This lack of quantification limits the validation of levels or modifications that could happen on the surface. Also batch
variability on uptake efficiency by macrophages was not addressed.
Given this reviewer’s thoughts that the proposed urgent need for the diagnostic tool of nanoparticle with 3 different imaging
modality possibilities combined is not consistent with clinical need, the focus really should be on the therapeutic benefits of
this approach. The investigators suggest ways this may be the case- and provide some evidence for improved targeting. The
investigators do compare the most functional version of their nano-particle to free atorvastatin. They report 3 animals per
group, and a significant difference. It is not clear how the dose was established for atorvastatin- and how this compared to
levels in clinical practice. It is well reported and wonderful to see the half-life in circulation, but tissue-specific distribution is
not quantitatively reported. To claim the plaque specific delivery and reduced off target effects reported, including
quantitation by fluorescence or radiolabelling in plaque vs organs(liver/spleen) is suggested.
The investigators state their approach “facilitates the targeted delivery of the ROS-scavenging
polymer and AT into plaque foam cells for synergistic treatment”. It is not generally
understood that atorvastatin or any statin has direct mechanism of benefit within the foam cell
( vs targetting HMGCoreductase in the liver). Whilst off-target, non-specific effects have been
proposed- this needs further introduction and discussion. For translational relevance, it is
suggested to consider immunological profiling beyond cytokines focussing on T-cell
activation after repeated dosing in animal model. Also, the study heavily emphasize on H₂O₂ as H₂O₂ is only one of the several ROS species elevated. Expanding ROS profiling to
other superoxides, peroxides and including relevant ROS scavenger controls is needed to confirm
ROS specific CD47 effects.
Overall strengths and additional comments in addition to above:
- Beautifully written with clear linkage between each method and its corresponding result. Sophisticated imaging validation.
- Beautiful graphical abstract and well written logical progression from molecular design to diagnostic and therapeutic
application.
- The finding that macrophage membrane coating and PS-binding peptide modification significantly facilitated the transport
of NPs across the inflamed endothelial barrier and their subsequent internalization by foam cells- is of interest and potential
broader relevance for atherosclerosis.
- Use of appropriate models- in vitro, ApoE−/− mouse model. In Figure 5- why is the
apoe-/e- mouse only having carotid
plaque detected? What about the classic finding of atherosclerosis in the arch of the aorta? Also- why is there only 1 visible
dot of uptake- not bilateral uptake?
- From a statistical perspective- there appear to only be n=3 of each treatment group- which
seems to be below what would be appropriate for the tests used.

### Reviewer 4

The authors construct a multifunctional molecular probe capable of simultaneously generating near-infrared II (NIR-II)
fluorescence, photoacoustic (PA), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) signals to enable comprehensive,
multidimensional assessment of AS plaques. They claim this probe can achieve on-demand release of atorvastatin within
foam cells promotes lipid efflux and reduces CD47 expression and thereby enhances macrophage-mediated phagocytosis,
after coupled with atorvastatin, encapsulated in responsive carriers, camouflaged with macrophage membranes, and
functionalized with a foam cell-targeting peptide.

1）The authors use a phosphatidylserine-targeting peptide (PS-binding peptide) to mediate the targeted delivery of FA-
P@MC to foam cells. However, since PS is externalized to the external leaflet in all apototic cells, the PS-targeting peptide
(CLIKKPF) used in this study binds not only to foam cells but also to other apototic cells in theory. Fig. 5f,g data also indicate
that FA-P@M and FA-P@MC were not only detected in carotid plaques but also highly accumulated in liver and less
accumulated in spleen and other tissues. Thus, the rationale using PS-binding peptide to target foam cells seems to be
unreasonable in this case.
2）In vitro anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects section, the authors state that FA-P@MC treatment markedly
suppressed foam cell formation in comparison to other groups, likely due to the therapeutic effect of AT in promoting lipid
efflux. This speculation is not convincing. The authors need to clarify the underlying mechanism by which FA-P@MC can
functionally promote lipid efflux in foam cells, and identify the transporter/receptors that mediate cholesterol efflux in foam
cells in this case.
Minor concerns:
3）Preparation of macrophage membrane and fabrication of FA-P@MC section. The targeting molecule (DSPE-PEG-
CLIKKPF) was synthesized according to our previous protocol. Please cite the reference.
4）List of abbreviations needed to be added.

4. Please clarify whether all experimental mice were fed the same high-fat diet throughout the
study. A detailed description of the composition and source of the high-fat diet would help in

Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. All experimental mice used in
this study were maintained on the same HDF throughout the experimental period to ensure
consistency. The HFD was purchased from SPF (Beijing) Biotechnology Co., Ltd and
consisted of 21.2% lard, 49.1% carbohydrate, 19.8% protein, and 0.2% cholesterol by weight,
a formulation widely used for establishing atherosclerosis models. The detailed composition
and supplier information have now been included in the revised Methods section to facilitate
reproducibility and better support the robustness of our experimental model.
5. There appears to be an inconsistency between the 790 nm excitation used for PA imaging
and the 808 nm excitation for fluorescence imaging. The rationale for selecting these two
close but distinct wavelengths should be addressed.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. The selection of
790 nm for PA imaging and 808 nm for fluorescence imaging were based on a careful
optimization of both the probe’s optical properties and the availability of excitation sources.
Specifically, 790 nm was chosen for PA imaging because it aligns with the probe’s absorption
peak and corresponds to a strong photoacoustic signal, as confirmed by PA spectroscopy,
making 790 nm the optimal choice for high-contrast PA imaging. For NIR-II fluorescence
imaging, 808 nm excitation was selected because commercially available lasers at this
wavelength provide efficient excitation, and the probe also showed strong absorption at
808 nm, enabling effective fluorescence emission.
Thus, the slight difference in excitation wavelengths reflects a balance between optimal
molecular signal performance and instrumental availability. This strategy is consistent with
previous reports in the literatures; for example, ACS Nano 2017, 11, 12276 employed 700 nm
excitation for PA imaging and 808 nm excitation for fluorescence imaging in vivo. We have
clarified this rationale in the revised Methods section to address the reviewer’s concern.

2. In Fig. 1c, the fluorescence intensity of the compounds increases in THF/water mixtures
with a water fraction up to 95%. The authors should explain this phenomenon.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer’s insightful question. The observed fluorescence
enhancement of the compound in THF/water mixtures with high water fractions is attributed
to the aggregation-induced emission (AIE) effect, a characteristic photophysical property of
our designed molecule. Unlike conventional fluorophores that exhibit aggregation-caused
quenching effect, AIE-active molecules are non-emissive or weakly emissive in solution but
become highly fluorescent upon aggregation (Nat. Commun. 2023, 14, 5216). In good
solvents (such as THF), the AIE molecules are weakly emissive due to non-radiative energy
dissipation through intramolecular motions. As the fraction of a poor solvent, such as water,
increases, the compound’s solubility decreases, leading to molecular aggregation.
Aggregation restricts intramolecular motions, suppressing non-radiative decay pathways and
promoting radiative transitions, which results in a marked increase in fluorescence intensity.
This AIE-induced fluorescence enhancement is a photophysical characteristic of our probe
and suggests its suitability for imaging in aqueous biological environments.

now been clearly indicated in the figure caption of the revised manuscript.

5. In addition to the responsive polymer, the authors added DSPE-PEG to the system. What is
the role of this polymer?
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this important question. In our system,
DSPE-PEG was introduced during nanoparticle preparation via the nanoprecipitation method
to function as a stabilizing surfactant. Owing to its amphiphilic structure, DSPE-PEG anchors
its hydrophobic lipid tail within the nanoparticle core while presenting a hydrophilic PEG
corona on the surface (Nat. Commun. 2022, 13, 758; ACS Nano 2023, 17, 955). This
prevents excessive aggregation of the hydrophobic probe and the ROS-responsive polymer,
thereby promoting uniform nanoparticle formation and enhancing colloidal stability. The
corresponding explanation has also been added to the revised Methods section.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The investigators have performed an elegant biomedical engineering feat- with a single
molecule can be used for molecular imaging to detect early atherosclerosis with 3 separate
advanced imaging modalities- MRI, NIR-II, and photoacoustic imaging.
They also perform elegant experiments in mouse models to demonstrate efficacy. This
manuscript presents a scientifically rigorous and impactful study, with strong translational
potential. Addressing the mechanistic and quantitative gaps would significantly strengthen
the manuscript’s clarity.
Response: We sincerely appreciate your positive feedback and insightful comments on our
work. Your constructive and professional suggestions have greatly enhanced the quality of
our manuscript. Below, we provide detailed responses to each of your comments.
My major concern is that this tool and approach does not take into consideration the reality of
screening for early atherosclerosis. The biggest cause of cardiovascular mortality is coronary
artery disease. If a patient is asymptomatic- screening even with established techniques as
CACS, CT coronary angiography (+/- with photon counting capabilities) has yet to be
accepted. The proposal that a major unmet need is optimizing the performance of a molecular
imaging contrast agent for use in all three modalities of MRI, NIR-II and photoacoustic
imaging is a “significant challenge” relevant to screening and treating early CAD is not well
founded or backed up by reference to the current clinical literature. Whilst carotid or
peripheral artery disease may have some chances in the near future with techniques such as
these- this fails to accurately predict CAD and CAD-related MI/death. Thus, my concern is
that this theranostic tool may not be addressing a question that we need addressed from a
diagnostic perspective.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We fully agree that
early screening for coronary artery disease (CAD) in asymptomatic patients remains highly
challenging. As the reviewer mentioned, even well-established modalities such as CACS and
CT coronary angiography are not yet widely accepted in this context, as they are usually less
sensitive for detecting non-calcified plaques and are constrained by radiation exposure and
cost, which restrict repeated monitoring in high-risk populations—particularly since
early-stage atherosclerosis often lacks calcification (Cardiovasc. Interv. Ther. 2025, 40, 536;
Circ. Cardiovasc. Interv. 2025, 28, e015529).
In this study, our goal was to establish a proof-of-concept multimodal molecular imaging
strategy integrating MRI, NIR-II FL, and photoacoustic imaging for multidimensional
evaluation of atherosclerosis. For feasibility assessment, we primarily focused on carotid
atherosclerosis, which are widely used in proof-of-concept studies and are
pathophysiologically relevant to systemic atherosclerosis and CAD risk. Our results
demonstrated that integrating complementary imaging modalities within one probe enhance
diagnostic accuracy and sensitivity by providing comprehensive, high-resolution insights into
plaque. A key advantage of our platform is that it targets foam cells and combines
complementary imaging modalities within a single molecular probe. As such, it is not
dependent on calcification and does not involve ionizing radiation, potentially overcoming
some of the limitations of current approaches for early-stage plaque monitoring.
To further address the reviewer’s comments, we conducted preliminary experiments to
explore the potential applicability of the platform in CAD. Early results suggested that our
platform-based NIR-II fluorescence imaging could be applied to visualize coronary stenosis
in high-fat diet-fed ApoE⁻/⁻ mice (Figure 1a,b). Histological analyses (H&E and ORO
staining) confirmed coronary plaque formation and lipid accumulation (Figure 1c-f), with
NIR-II signal correlating with plaque burden. These findings demonstrate the potential of
extending this imaging strategy to coronary models.
Overall, the current study provides a proof-of-concept demonstrating the feasibility of a foam
cell-targeted multimodal imaging platform for atherosclerosis diagnosis. Moving forward, we
plan to further optimize the imaging probe and multimodal acquisition protocols to further
improve sensitivity and specificity for CAD detection, thereby bridging the gap between
preclinical AS models and clinically relevant coronary imaging. In the revised manuscript, we
have expanded the discussion to clarify these points (new Supplementary Fig. 56, page 34).

In regard to potential therapeutic value of the tool, the investigators state that: probe, coupled
with atorvastatin, is encapsulated in responsive carriers, further camouflaged with
macrophage membranes, and functionalized with a foam cell-targeting peptide. The
hierarchical targeting strategy leverages the biomimetic affinity of macrophages for inflamed
plaques and the selective targeting of foam cells through a phosphatidylserine (PS)-binding
peptide, ensuring precise foam cell navigation. The on-demand release of atorvastatin within
foam cells promotes lipid efflux and reduces CD47 expression, thereby enhancing
macrophage-mediated phagocytosis. This intervention effectively inhibits plaque progression,
alleviates inflammation burden, and stabilizes plaques in AS mouse models”.
This sounds fantastic, however, most of the steps outlined in this, and what is shown in the
graphical abstract, is not backed with specific experimental data and appropriate controls, and
is theoretical, based on the engineering. Eg. “while the targeting peptide directs the system to
foam cells within plaques. Atorvastatin release within foam cells promotes lipid efflux and
reduces CD47 expression, thereby enhancing macrophage-mediated phagocytosis”. Causality
is implied here regarding the specific targeting release of atorvastatin within foam cells
promotes the lipid efflux and reduces CD47, thereby enhancing macrophage- mediated
phagocytosis. There are many layers of this that need specific control to declare causality.
These are not well described in the abstract, or the graphical abstract.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the thoughtful suggestions and constructive
comments highlighting the importance of providing more detailed experiment evidence to
support the causal relationships proposed in our study. In response, we have reorganized the
data presentation and performed additional experiments to address these concerns, as outlined
below:
1. Targeting and uptake by foam cells: We demonstrated that FA-P@MC could efficiently
traverse the inflammatory endothelial barrier and be preferentially internalized by foam cells
(Figure 2a–f in the manuscript). These results provide direct evidence that the nanoplatform
possesses foam cell–targeting capability, establishing the basis for drug delivery to foam
cells.
2. Effects on lipid uptake: We have demonstrated that FA-P@MC treatment significantly
reduced lipid uptake by foam cells using ORO staining (Figure 2g,h in the manuscript). To
further validate this effect, we performed additional experiments using DiI-labelled oxLDL.
Fluorescence imaging confirmed that oxLDL uptake in the FA-P@MC group was
1.84–4.65-folds lower than those in the other treatment groups (Figure 2a-b below).
To further elucidate the underlying mechanism, we conducted additional experiments
examining the expression of key lipid uptake receptors. Our results indicated that FA-P@MC
treatment downregulated the scavenger receptors CD36 and LOX-1 relative to control
treatments, which are known to mediate oxLDL internalization, thereby limiting lipid
accumulation in foam cells (Figure 2c-f below).
3. Effects on cholesterol efflux: To further investigate cholesterol efflux, we analyzed the
culture supernatant from foam cells following different treatments. Quantitative analysis
revealed a significant increase in cholesterol efflux in the supernatant from
FA-P@MC–treated group compared with PBS controls and other groups (Figure 3a). In
addition, immunofluorescence staining demonstrated upregulation of SR-BI and ABCA1,
two
critical transporters involved in cholesterol efflux (Figure 3b–e). These results indicate that
FA-P@MC promotes cholesterol efflux in foam cells by enhancing the expression of efflux
transporters.
4. Regulation of CD47 expression and phagocytosis：Both in vitro and in vivo analyses,
including Western blotting and immunofluorescence staining, demonstrated that targeted
atorvastatin delivery via FA-P@MC significantly downregulated CD47 expression on foam
cells (Figure 3a–c, Figure 7h–j in the manuscript). Functionally, this downregulation was
associated with enhanced phagocytic clearance of foam cells by macrophages, as confirmed
through immunofluorescence imaging and quantitative flow cytometry analysis (Figure 3d–g
in the manuscript).
5. In vivo enhanced plaque delivery: Both the in vivo multimodel imaging and ex imaging of
harvested carotid samples indicated the FA-P@MC had improved targeting toward the plaque
lesion compared to the non-targeted nanoformulations.
We further conducted additional experiment indicated that FA-P@MC can penetrate into
plaques and be preferentially uptake by foam cells (Figure 4 below). Additionally,
quantitative analysis of drug accumulation in plaque tissues was conducted, which also
confirmed that the FA-P@MC group had a higher AT content within plaques compared with
non-targeting control formulations (Figure 5 below), indicating the enhanced drug delivery to
plaques.
6. In vivo therapeutic outcomes: In ApoE⁻/⁻ mice, ORO staining of the aortic arch and H&E
staining demonstrated that FA-P@MC treatment significantly reduced plaque progression
compared with other groups. Analyses of inflammatory cytokines and immune cell
infiltration indicated that FA-P@MC mitigated plaque-associated inflammation.
Immunohistochemical staining also suggested improved plaque stability following treatment.
To corroborate these findings, we further performed additional ORO staining of the aortic
root and biochemical assays, which confirmed that FA-P@MC administration markedly
reduced plaque lipid content and total cholesterol levels (Figures 6, 7 below). These results
are consistent with the observed modulation of lipid uptake, enhanced cholesterol efflux, and
foam cell clearance, collectively supporting the therapeutic efficacy of FA-P@MC in
attenuating atherosclerotic plaque development.
Together, these results provide experimental support for the sequential pathway we proposed:
targeted delivery of atorvastatin into foam cells → reduced lipid uptake and enhanced
cholesterol efflux → downregulation of CD47 → improved phagocytic clearance →
attenuation of plaque burden. These new results and corresponding discussions have been
added to the revised manuscript (new Supplementary Fig. 33-34, page 14; new
Supplementary Fig. 46-50, pages 21, 27). We sincerely thank the reviewer for these
constructive comments, which have substantially strengthened our study.

Given this reviewer’s thoughts that the proposed urgent need for the diagnostic tool of
nanoparticle with 3 different imaging modality possibilities combined is not consistent with
clinical need, the focus really should be on the therapeutic benefits of this approach. The
investigators suggest ways this may be the case- and provide some evidence for improved
targeting. The investigators do compare the most functional version of their nano-particle to
free atorvastatin. They report 3 animals per group, and a significant difference. It is not clear

Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for these constructive comments and suggestions.
Regarding the dosing strategy, for the clinical prevention and management of cardiovascular
disease, statins are mainly administered orally at doses ranging from 10–80 mg/day. To allow
comparison with our animal studies, we referred to the FDA-recommended body surface area
conversion method to estimate the human equivalent dose. The dose of 3 mg/kg used in our
ApoE⁻/⁻ mouse model corresponds to approximately 14 mg for a 60 kg adult, which falls
within the clinically relevant range. Additionally, our regimen (3 mg/kg, twice weekly,
intravenously) is lower than those used for several previously reported intravenous nano-AT
formulations in animal studies (e.g., 7 mg/kg, twice weekly in J. Control. Release 2018, 283,
241; 8.5 mg/kg every other day in Nanoscale 2020, 12, 9541), yet it still achieved efficient
therapeutic benefit. Thus, the dosing strategy we adopted provides a reasonable assessment of
the therapeutic potential of our system.
To assess tissue distribution and plaque targeting, we further performed biodistribution
studies using Cy5-labelled AT. Different formulations were intravenously injected into
ApoE⁻/⁻ mice, and major organs as well as the aorta were harvested at 12 h post-injection for
analysis. In the AT alone group, only weak fluorescence was detected in the aorta, consistent
with the rapid clearance of small-molecule AT (Figure 9a,b). In contrast, FA-P@MC
demonstrated markedly enhanced accumulation in aortic plaques compared with the
non-targeted FA-P@M and free AT groups. To further confirm these findings, we quantified
the AT content in different tissues through homogenization and extraction. Both FA-P@M
and FA-P@MC exhibited notable liver distribution due to nanoparticle uptake by the
reticuloendothelial system, consistent with common nanoparticle biodistribution patterns.
Importantly, the drug concentrations in plaque tissues of FA-P@MC group were
approximately 12.7-fold higher than free AT and about 2-fold higher than FA-P@M group
(Figure 10). Together, these results provide evidence of improved plaque delivery of AT via
FA-P@MC, consistent with its therapeutic advantage. The data have been added to the
revised manuscript (new Supplementary Fig. 45 and Fig. 46) and discussed accordingly (page
21).

Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for these insightful suggestions. While the
primary therapeutic effect of atorvastatin is usually mediated via inhibition of HMG-CoA
reductase in the liver, increasing evidence indicates that it can also exert local effects within
the vascular walls and immune cells, including modulation of cholesterol efflux and
anti-inflammatory activity (Clin. Rev. Allergy Immunol. 2020, 60, 175; Nat. Rev. Immunol.
2006, 6, 358). Consistent with these reports, both our in vitro and in vivo experimental data
indicated that AT can effectively reduce lipid uptake, enhance cholesterol efflux in foam cells,
and reduce the foam cells, thus alleviating the plaque burdens. According to the reviewer’s
suggestion, we have included a related discussion in the revised manuscript (page 7).
To further address the reviewer’s comments regarding immunological profiling on T cells,
we
evaluated T cell populations within atherosclerotic plaques from different treatment groups. T
lymphocytes, recruited by antigen-presenting cells, are closely associated with lesion
inflammation. During plaque progression, CD4+ and CD8+ T cells generally increase and
secret pro-inflammatory cytokines, whereas regulatory T cells (Tregs) are relatively low or
insufficient, providing limited anti-inflammatory control (Nat. Med. 2019, 25, 1576;
Immunobiology 2016, 22, 1014; Life 2023, 13, 1931). In the FA-P@MC–treated group, the
proportions of CD8+ and CD4+ T cells within plaques were found to reduce by approximately
4.68- and 2.53-fold, respectively, compared with the model group, as determined by flow
cytometry (Figure 11a-c). In contrast, the number of CD25+Foxp3+ Treg cells in the
FA-P@MC group increased by approximately 5.19-fold relative to the model group (Figure
11d,e).
These changes in T cell composition were consistent with the observed reduction in
pro-inflammatory cytokines reported in our manuscript. Collectively, these findings suggest
that FA-P@MC treatment can further affect T cell populations within plaques, providing
additional insight into its immunomodulatory effects. The data have been added to the revised
manuscript (new Supplementary Fig. 53) and discussed accordingly (page 32).

Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors construct a multifunctional molecular probe capable of simultaneously
generating near-infrared II (NIR-II) fluorescence, photoacoustic (PA), and magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) signals to enable comprehensive, multidimensional assessment of
AS plaques. They claim this probe can achieve on-demand release of atorvastatin within
foam cells promotes lipid efflux and reduces CD47 expression and thereby enhances
macrophage-mediated phagocytosis, after coupled with atorvastatin, encapsulated in
responsive carriers, camouflaged with macrophage membranes, and functionalized with a
foam cell-targeting peptide.
Response: We sincerely thank you for your positive feedback and insightful comments on
our work. Your constructive suggestions have significantly improved the quality of our
manuscript. Below, we provide detailed responses to each of your comments.
Major concerns:
1）The authors use a phosphatidylserine-targeting peptide (PS-binding peptide) to mediate the
targeted delivery of FA-P@MC to foam cells. However, since PS is externalized to the
external leaflet in all apototic cells, the PS-targeting peptide (CLIKKPF) used in this study
binds not only to foam cells but also to other apototic cells in theory. Fig. 5f, g data also
indicate that FA-P@M and FA-P@MC were not only detected in carotid plaques but also
highly accumulated in liver and less accumulated in spleen and other tissues. Thus, the
rationale using PS-binding peptide to target foam cells seems to be unreasonable in this case.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this thoughtful and important comment. In
our design, the macrophage membrane coating endows the nanoplatform with inflammatory
plaque-homing capability, while the PS-targeting peptide (CLIKKPF) was introduced to
further enhance selective recognition of foam cells. Unlike transient PS exposure in classical
apoptotic cells, foam cells within atherosclerotic plaques exhibit prolonged and amplified PS
exposure. Mechanistically, lipid peroxidation in foam cells inactivates flippases and activates
scramblases, leading to largely irreversible PS exposure (Nat. Commun. 2020, 11, 4646),
while inflammatory signaling (e.g., TNF-α/NF-κB) further suppresses PS internalization
(Cell Death Dis. 2018, 9, 261). Consequently, PS-targeting peptides have been adopted as a
feasible strategy to enhance foam cell–specific delivery within plaques (J. Am. Chem. Soc.
2024, 146, 10093; Adv. Sci. 2024, 11, 2307441).
Regarding the biodistribution results (Fig. 5f,g), the liver accumulation is primarily due to
reticuloendothelial system (RES) clearance, a phenomenon commonly observed for most
nanomedicines (Adv. Drug Deliv. Rev. 2020, 165–166, 1–14; J. Control. Release 2018, 270,
165). Importantly, in vivo fluorescence imaging demonstrated that FA-P@MC exhibited
obviously higher plaque accumulation than non-PS-targeted FA-P@M, despite both
formulations experiencing liver uptake. Quantitative analysis of drug accumulation in plaque
tissues was further conducted, which also confirmed that the FA-P@MC group had a higher
AT content within plaques compared with FA-P@M, indicating that PS-targeting
modification enhanced drug delivery to plaques.
While these findings support the rationale that the PS-binding peptide improves plaque
enrichment, we also acknowledge the reviewer’s point that PS exposure is not entirely unique
to foam cells, which actually reflects a broader challenge shared by many targeting strategies.
In future work, we plan to explore more specific ligands to further enhance both the
selectivity and efficiency of plaque targeting. The results have been added (new
Supplementary Fig. 46) and discussed in the revised manuscript (page 21).

2）In vitro anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects section, the authors state that
FA-P@MC treatment markedly suppressed foam cell formation in comparison to other
groups, likely due to the therapeutic effect of AT in promoting lipid efflux. This speculation is
not convincing. The authors need to clarify the underlying mechanism by which FA-P@MC
can functionally promote lipid efflux in foam cells, and identify the transporter/receptors that
mediate cholesterol efflux in foam cells in this case.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. Following the
reviewer’s suggestion, we further investigated the mechanism by which FA-P@MC inhibits
foam cell formation and promotes lipid/cholesterol efflux by examining the expression of
relevant transporters and receptors.
First, we found that FA-P@MC significantly inhibited oxLDL internalization by RAW cells.
As shown in Figure 2a,b, oxLDL uptake in the FA-P@MC group was 4.65–1.84-fold lower
than those in other groups. Mechanistic studies revealed that FA-P@MC treatment markedly
downregulated the expression of scavenger receptors CD36 and LOX-1 (Figure 2c–f), which
are key mediators of lipid internalization. These results indicate that FA-P@MC effectively
suppresses oxLDL uptake by modulating scavenger receptor expression.
In addition, FA-P@MC treatment enhanced cholesterol efflux from foam cells. The
cholesterol concentration in the supernatant increased by 8.6-fold compared with the PBS
group (Figure 3a). Immunofluorescence analysis further showed that the expression of the
efflux transporters SR-BI and ABCA1 was upregulated by 7.6-fold and 9-fold, respectively,
in FA-P@MC-treated cells (Figure 3b–e). These findings demonstrate that FA-P@MC not
only limits lipid uptake but also actively promotes cholesterol efflux via SR-BI and ABCA1,
thereby functionally suppressing foam cell formation.
The corresponding data have been added to the revised manuscript (new Supplementary Fig.
33, 34) and discussed in detail (page 14). We greatly appreciate the reviewer’s insightful
suggestion, which has significantly strengthened our study.
